image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Faceted density/distribution chart** (small multiples of overlaid smoothed distributions).
- Each panel shows temperature distributions for a city, with shaded regions highlighting unusually cold and unusually hot nights.

## 2. Layout techniques
- **Faceting / small multiples**: separate panels for different cities.
- **Layering/overplotting**: multiple filled distribution shapes are overlaid within each panel.
- **Reference lines**: vertical dotted lines mark thresholds for abnormal cold/hot.
- **Text annotations**: percentages and labels are placed directly on panels.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| City (Phoenix, Las Vegas, San Francisco, New Orleans, Houston, Chicago, Atlanta, New York (JFK), Washington) | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title |
| Summer minimum temperature (°F) | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Frequency / distribution of nights | Quantitative | Height/shape of filled density area (y-position/area) |
| Time period: 1960s | Temporal | Fill color (light gray) and direct label |
| Time period: 2020s | Temporal | Fill color (orange/pink shaded distribution) and direct label |
| Abnormally cold nights | Categorical/derived | Blue shaded tail area to the left of cold threshold; annotation text |
| Abnormally hot nights | Categorical/derived | Pink/red shaded tail area to the right of hot threshold; annotation text |
| Cold threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Hot threshold | Quantitative/derived | Vertical dotted reference line |
| Percent of nights abnormally cold | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |
| Percent of nights abnormally hot | Quantitative | Text annotation inside each panel |

I notice that the minimum daily temperatures between June and August have increased for every city depicted in these graphs when compared to the 1960s. I also take note that the percentage of days considered “abnormally hot” is always significantly higher than days considered “abnormally cold” for these cities. For example, in Phoenix, less than 1% of nights have been abnormally cold yet 49% of the days were abnormally hot, and Chicago has seen less than 1% abnormally cold days and 61% abnormally hot ones.
I wonder what has caused these increases in temperature, especially considering that these are minimum temperatures being recorded. I wonder if this something that we as humans can avoid or reverse,  and if these such increases are avoidable, what practices should be abandoned because they contribute to an overall spike in minimum summer night temperature.
The findings of these graphs relate to my community and me because we are the ones living through these times and trends. Additionally, hotter temperatures contribute to detrimental health issues, such as heat stroke, heat exhaustion, and sunburn, while also raising the need for energy for air conditioning, possibly resulting in money loss.
An appropriate headline for this graph is: “Don’t Blame It on Me, Blame it on the Night: Why do Minimum Nighttime Summer Temperatures Seem to be Increasing?”

Today’s graphs show the distributions of the daily summer minimum night temperatures in nine U.S. cities for the 1960s decade and the 2020s decade to date.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the online article that included these graphs plus an interactive feature that animates for the seven decades since 1960 the distributions of temperatures for all cities with airports.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response (and replies made to it) to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex),

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, May 6 with moderation on Wednesday, May 11.  The topic – teen behaviors.  The May 11 graph will be the last “What’s Going On In This Graph?” for the school year.  Keep noticing and wondering.

This is really a shock to me, because even though I knew that global warming is a big problem, I didn't know that it could completely change our average temperatures in only 60 years.

Don't think that global warming exists? Look at these graphs and think again!
